blocks.text: But Sextus Empiricus, book 1, says otherwise: Τὸ γοῦν κώνειον πιαίνει τοὺς ὄρτυγας [to goun kōneion piainei tous ortygas]. Hemlock fattens quails. Others report this of the starling. And the Arabs, again, say otherwise. Alkazuinius, under The Quail: يغتدي بالبيش والبيش [yaghtadī bi-l-bīsh wa-l-bīsh] [col. 98] هو سم قاتل [huwa samm qātil] It feeds on napellus, which is a deadly poison. Avicenna, in the chapter بيش [bīsh], that is On napellus: والسماني يغتدي به ولا يموت منه [wa-l-summānā yaghtadī bihi wa-lā yamūtu minhu] Quails feed on it, and yet do not die from it. The same is in Alcamus. Napellus, however, is neither hellebore nor hemlock, but aconite, λυκοκτόνον [lykoktonon]. However that may be, all agree that quails feed on poisons. And for that very reason not a few forbid them as unwholesome. Pliny, book 10, ch. 23: To quails the seed of poison is the most welcome food; for which reason they have banished them from the table. And following him Solinus: Their most welcome food is the seeds of poisonous plants; for which reason the tables of the prudent have banished them. Didymus in the Geoponica, book 14: Οἱ ὄρτυγες, ἐλλέβορον ἐπινεμόμενοι, τοὺς ἐσθίοντας εἰς κίνδυνον ἐμβάλλουσι, κατατεινομένους, καὶ ἰλιγγιῶντας· [Hoi ortyges, elleboron epinemomenoi, tous esthiontas eis kindynon emballousi, katateinomenous, kai ilingiōntas] Quails that feed on hellebore bring those who eat them into such danger that they are distended and convulsed, as if seized by vertigo ^{(1)}. Avicenna, however, attributes this not so much to their eating hellebore as [II, 658] to a bad quality inherent in them. His words are in book 2 of the Canon, in the chapter سماني [summānī], that is On the quail: اكل لحمه يخاف منه التمدد والتشنج لا لانه ياكل الخربق فقط بل لان في جوهره هذه القوة واظن ان اغتداه بالخربق هو والمشاكلة المزاج [akl laḥmihi yukhāfu minhu al-tamaddud wa-l-tashannuj lā li-annahu yaʾkulu al-kharbaq faqaṭ bal li-anna fī jawharihi hādhihi al-quwwa wa-aẓunnu anna ightidāʾahu bi-l-kharbaq huwa wa-l-mushākala al-mizāj] From eating its flesh tetanus and spasm are to be feared, not only because it eats hellebore, but also because this property is inherent in its substance; indeed I think it feeds on hellebore precisely because this food suits its temperament. From Pliny and Solinus it is added that it is customary to spit at it on account of the falling sickness, which alone of animals, apart from man, they fear. Rasis, however, says something very different in his book to Almansor, in the chapter On the flesh of birds, which is the tenth of the third treatise: The flesh of the starna (the partridge) is found to be lighter than the flesh of any other bird, and so more suitable for those who wish to be kept on a delicate regimen. After it the flesh of the quail stands second in goodness. And a little later: The flesh of chickens likewise is placed after it. The flesh of the quail, however, is more productive of good blood, and increases semen. And Ibnozohar, in the book On Foods, chapter On quails: وامزاجها فكانها وسط بين مزاج الدجاج والحجل وهي الي مزاج الدجاج اميل وهي الطف جوهرا واميل الي حر قليلا وهي جيدة الكيموص طيبة الطعم نافعه للاصحا والناقهين ولحومها تفتت الحصا وتدر البول [wa-amzājuhā fa-ka-annahā wasaṭ bayna mizāj al-dajāj wa-l-ḥajal wa-hiya ilā mizāj al-dajāj amyal wa-hiya alṭaf jawharan wa-amyal ilā ḥarr qalīlan wa-hiya jayyidat al-kaymūs ṭayyibat al-ṭaʿm nāfiʿa li-l-aṣiḥḥāʾ wa-l-nāqihīn wa-luḥūmuhā tufattitu al-ḥaṣā wa-tudirru al-bawl] It has a temperament roughly midway between the hen and the partridge, yet so that it comes closer to the temperament of the hen. But its substance is finer, and inclines a little more to the hot. It also yields good chyme and has an excellent flavour, and is beneficial to the healthy and strong. And its flesh breaks up the stone and promotes urine. And in the last century Nicolaus Massa, in his Medical Letters, cited by Gesner: Quails, [col. 99] that is, qualeae, are of the same temperament as partridges, but drier. They nourish well. And Aloysius Mundella: Aristotle treats of quails and partridges in the same chapter, as if the two did not differ much in nature. Therefore, since they seem to be of the same kind, it remains clear that the quail is not, as is commonly said, of bad juice, nor to be banished from the table, except perhaps that of the poor, who are accustomed to eat cheaper foods. Nor would I judge that one should abstain from eating it because it is seized by the falling sickness, or because it feeds on poison. For we know some animals which, although they are sometimes nourished by poisons, nevertheless produce good and harmless juice. For example, starlings feed on hemlock, as the same Galen attests; who does not eat them without harm? [II, 659] nourished, are nevertheless of good juice, like starlings, which feed on hemlock. And if the quail does feed on hellebore, which is not yet established for us, it is more probable that it is helped by that food than harmed. Therefore I judge that the nourishment of the quail, which is also of no unpleasant flavour, is to be praised rather than condemned. For Averroes too praises the flesh of quails wonderfully, as producing good juice. And although they sometimes feed on poison, and are sometimes afflicted with the falling sickness, I think this is not always so, nor true of all, but perhaps of those that are caught and kept in aviaries. For on this reasoning cocks too would have to be rejected, because some of them are sometimes seized by the falling sickness. Nor would I pass over this: that the Lord our God would not have fed the people of Israel, whom he loved most ardently, with quails to the point of satiety while they passed through those desert places, had they not been an approved and wholesome food. So Mundella, and more, which the reader may see there. And if one wishes to go further back, it will appear that the makers of myths thought highly of the quail, since they relate that Hercules, slain by Typhon, was recalled to life by the smell of a quail brought to him by Iolaus, and that this is why the Phoenicians sacrificed quails to him. Athenaeus, book 9: Εὔδοξος δὲ ὁ Κνίδιος ἐν πρώτῳ γῆς περιόδου τοὺς Φοίνικας λέγει θύειν τῷ Ἡρακλεῖ ὄρτυγας, διὰ τὸ τὸν Ἡρακλέα, τὸν Ἀστερίας καὶ Διὸς, πορευόμενον εἰς Λιβύην, ἀναιρεθῆναι μὲν ὑπὸ Τυφῶνος. Ἰολάου δ᾽ αὐτῷ προσενέγκαντος ὄρτυγα, καὶ προσαγάγοντος, ὀσφρανθέντα ἀναβιῶναι. [Eudoxos de ho Knidios en prōtō gēs periodou tous Phoinikas legei thyein tō Hēraklei ortygas, dia to ton Hērakléa, ton Asterias kai Dios, poreuomenon eis Libyēn, anairethēnai men hypo Typhōnos. Iolaou d᾽ autō prosenenkantos ortyga, kai prosagagontos, osphranthenta anabiōnai.] This gave rise to a proverb current among the Greeks,
